newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's KDD in big cable project to aid expansion.
newsitem.headline: Japan's KDD in big cable project to aid expansion.

text.p: Japan's biggest international phone company, KDD, said Thursday it will invest about $900 million to lay an undersea optical fiber cable as part of its push into the Japanese domestic phone market.

Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co. Ltd. said its "Japan Information Highway" cable looping around Japan's three main islands would also help cut the cost of international call charges, often blamed by foreigners for high business costs in Japan.
The 5,312 mile cable will carry 1.2 million phone lines and is scheduled to go into use by mid-1999.
KDD is investing in the cable to give it the capacity it needs to expand into the domestic phone call sector, now largely dominated by the giant Nippon Telegraph & Telephone Corp.

KDD said that, through the investment, it was positioning itself for entry into the lucrative domestic phone business. It is now barred by Japanese law from offering domestic phone services but is expected to obtain approval by next summer.
"We would move into domestic services after the law is amended," KDD president Tadashi Nishimoto told a news conference.

KDD's entry into domestic services would be another big headache for NTT, the world's biggest phone company, which is already facing tough competition with foreign and domestic firms gearing up to enter the home call market.
Nishimoto said the cable would enable KDD to offer domestic long-distance call services more cheaply than NTT, because it was cheaper to lay the cable under the sea than on land.

The investment would also enable the company to lower its international rates by cutting the yearly access charges it pays to NTT by 10 billion yen ($90.0 million) from the current 30 billion yen ($270 million).
"We hope to achieve the target of cutting charges for calls to the United States to 300 yen ($2) per minute earlier than our original target year of 2000," Nishimoto said.
KDD now charges 480 yen ($4) per minute for daytime calls.
Some analysts were sceptical, saying that KDD may be too late to enter the domestic long-distance call market as cut-throat rate competition has already started.
"KDD is only trying to obtain a good bargaining position in the coming merger and acquisition era," said Makio Inui, an analyst at Salomon Brothers.

In late August, there was a rumour in the Tokyo stock markets that KDD would merge with Japan Telecom Co. in order to survive in the competitive environment. Japan Telecom President Koichi Sakata quickly denied the rumours, but added that alliances would make more sense than a merger.
